lines.text: Why does every movie theater smell like popcorn? Funny thing is, it wasn't always welcome.
People have popped corn for thousands of years. In Peru, archaeologists found popcorn about six thousand seven hundred years old.
In eighteen eighty-five, Charles Cretors of Chicago built a steam-powered popcorn machine. Now vendors could pop it anywhere.
But the grand movie palaces kept it out. They had fancy carpets, and silent films meant reading title cards. They wanted a classy crowd.
Then, in nineteen twenty-seven, the talkies arrived, and everyone came to the movies.
When the Depression hit, a bag of popcorn cost a nickel or a dime. Theaters that started selling it stayed in business.
In World War Two, sugar rationing made candy scarce. Americans ate three times as much popcorn.
Today, a bucket costs the theater pennies to make, and it helps keep the lights on.
So popcorn didn't sneak into the movies. It saved them.
